Dear Waypoint Mobility Hiring Team,

I'm applying for the Data Scientist, Demand Forecasting role. For the past three years I've worked on transit ridership data, first preparing reports for transit planners and then building forecasting models. I'd like to keep doing that work at Waypoint, where forecasts reach planners in more than 40 cities. I finish my M.S. in Data Science at Lakeshore University in December 2026.

As a research assistant in Lakeshore's Urban Analytics Lab, I built bus ridership forecasting models with XGBoost and LightGBM. They used four years of automatic passenger counter data joined with anonymized third-party mobility data. I led the feature engineering and evaluation, and I'm first author on the resulting UrbanDS 2025 workshop paper. On a 2023 holdout, our model cut MAPE from 14.2% for a SARIMA seasonal baseline to 9.8%. The most useful features were the day of the week, the previous week's boardings, the school calendar, and a mobility index. A reviewer raised possible leakage from the one-week-lagged mobility features, so I re-ran the models with a two-week lag. Error rose to 10.4% but still clearly beat the baseline. That check shaped how I evaluate forecasts: I look for the assumptions that could make a model seem better than it is.

Before graduate school, I was a Data Analyst at Lakeshore Regional Transit Authority. I maintained the Tableau and SQL ridership dashboards used by the planning department. I also automated the weekly reporting pipeline in Python, which cut preparation time from about six hours to one. That job showed me what planners need from a number: it has to arrive on time, and they need to trust where it came from.

I've also learned to explain model results to people who don't build models. As a Data Science Intern at Northpoint Insurance this summer, I raised a churn model's validation AUC from 0.71 to 0.76 using gradient boosting and calibrated its probabilities. I then presented the results to the retention team and a VP, focusing on which customer segments the model flags and how outreach could be prioritized. As a TA for a statistics course for non-majors, I've spent two semesters explaining uncertainty to students who don't come from a technical background.

I haven't deployed a model to production yet. My churn model went to the retention analytics team for further evaluation. Working with engineering to get models into production is something I'm eager to do at Waypoint, and I already have the transit data experience and the habits around forecast evaluation that the role needs.

Thank you for your consideration. I'd welcome the chance to talk.

Sincerely,
Morgan Reyes

---

Some choices I made:
- **The paper is called a "workshop paper,"** not "peer-reviewed," because your CV lists it as non-archival. The HealthBridge letter called it "peer-reviewed," so you may want to change that one too.
- **Numbers are exact (14.2% → 9.8%)** instead of "over 30%." I also included the 10.4% result from the leakage check, since it shows careful evaluation.
- **I said plainly that you haven't deployed a model to production,** because the job lists it as a bonus and an interviewer would ask anyway.
- **The PhD isn't mentioned,** since it doesn't help this application.

# Statement of Purpose: Morgan Reyes
**PhD in Computer Science (Human-Computer Interaction), Khoury College of Computer Sciences, Fall 2027**

Five participants in a usability study I helped run last spring all accepted the AutoML tool's top-ranked model without checking its metrics. None of them opened the feature-importance panel. Two assumed the tool already "knew" which columns in their dataset were sensitive. They weren't careless. They were graduate students in data science who understood the tool's capabilities better than most of its intended users. What they had trouble with was the gap between what the system showed them and what it actually did.

I've watched that gap from both sides for three years, first as an analyst producing numbers for decision-makers and then as a researcher building the models behind them. I want to pursue a PhD in HCI to study it directly: **how people who don't build ML systems come to understand, trust, and act on what those systems produce, and how interfaces can help them rely on model outputs as much as those outputs deserve, and no more.**

## From producing numbers to wondering how they're read

After my B.A. in Economics, I worked for a year as a Data Analyst at Lakeshore Regional Transit Authority. I maintained the ridership dashboards that the planning department used and automated our weekly reporting pipeline. The technical work was simple. The hard part was that the same chart meant different things to different readers. When I redesigned a dashboard for the agency's board members, the main question wasn't which numbers to include. It was what a non-specialist would conclude from them, and whether that conclusion would be right.

I started my M.S. in Data Science partly to build better models, and I did. As a research assistant in Prof. S. Patel's Urban Analytics Lab, I developed gradient-boosted models to forecast bus ridership recovery, using four years of automatic passenger counter data and an anonymized mobility index. I led the feature engineering and evaluation and was first author on our UrbanDS 2025 workshop paper. Our model reduced MAPE from 14.2% for a seasonal baseline to 9.8% on a 2023 holdout. When a reviewer raised possible leakage from our lagged mobility features, I re-ran the analysis with a longer lag and reported the higher error, 10.4%, alongside the original.

That project taught me careful evaluation. It also showed me where my interest really was. Preparing the workshop talk, I framed the motivation around planners who face uncertainty about ridership recovery. Yet nothing in the paper said how a planner would read a 10% error, or whether SHAP plots would mean anything to the people deciding service levels. The modeling question was settled, but the human question hadn't been asked.

## Moving toward HCI

In Spring 2026 I took Human-Centered Data Science as an elective, and it gave me methods for the questions I'd been circling. My team of three ran think-aloud sessions with five classmates using an AutoML dashboard, and I wrote the findings section of our report. It was a small class project and isn't published, so I don't overstate what it shows. But the patterns we saw (participants deferring to the system's ranking, ignoring explanations they had access to, assuming safeguards that didn't exist) matched what I'd seen with planners and board members. That's when I understood these behaviors could be studied systematically, not just noticed.

This summer I tested the idea in a different setting. As a Data Science Intern at Northpoint Insurance, I built a churn model that raised validation AUC from 0.71 to 0.76 and calibrated its probabilities. Then I presented it to the retention team and a VP. Most of my preparation went into explaining what AUC does and doesn't mean, and into framing the outputs as decisions about which customers to contact first. I noticed that calibration, which I'd treated as a technical detail, was the part that most affected whether the audience could use the numbers correctly.

Teaching has given me a third view. For two semesters I've been a TA for STAT 1100, a statistics course for non-majors. When I designed the rubric for the final data project, I found that the "interpretation" criterion separated students far more than the "analysis" criterion did. Students could run the analysis correctly and still draw conclusions it didn't support.

## Research interests

I'm still forming my research agenda and expect a PhD to sharpen it. Right now I'm drawn to three related questions:

1. **Appropriate reliance on model outputs.** When non-expert decision-makers such as planners, analysts, or AutoML users are given predictions, rankings, or uncertainty estimates, what leads them to over-rely or under-rely? Which interface interventions actually change that?
2. **Communicating uncertainty for decisions.** Forecast error metrics are designed for modelers. How can uncertainty be presented so that it changes what a domain expert does, and not just what they say they understand?
3. **Mismatched mental models in automated tools.** Our participants assumed the AutoML tool handled sensitive attributes. How common are these assumptions about what ML tools do on users' behalf, and how should tools correct them?

My background is mostly quantitative, and I see that as a strength for this work. I can build the systems I'd be studying, design evaluations that hold up to scrutiny, and analyze behavioral data rigorously. What I need, and what I'm applying to Khoury for, is training in qualitative and mixed methods, study design, and HCI theory, so that I can go from noticing these patterns to explaining them.

## Why Khoury

[**To fill in:** name 1–3 Khoury HCI faculty whose work matches the questions above, and add a sentence on a specific paper or project of theirs and how your interests connect. I didn't name anyone, because I'd rather you choose based on papers you've actually read than have me guess.]

I'm also drawn to Khoury's interdisciplinary setting. My questions sit between ML, visualization, and the study of how people make decisions, and I want a program where those areas talk to each other.

## Looking ahead

I finish my M.S. in December 2026. Long term, I want to do research that changes how ML tools are designed for the people who use their outputs, not only the people who build them, whether in academia or an industry research lab. I've spent three years making numbers more accurate. I want to spend the next several years understanding what happens after those numbers reach the people who use them.

---

Things you should know before using this:

- **The faculty paragraph is a placeholder.** I didn't search for or name specific professors. A good fit paragraph needs papers you've actually read, so pick them yourself.
- **The research questions are my own framing.** You told me you weren't sure of a topic beyond "something with people and AI, not just building models," so I built one from your experiences. Make sure it reflects what you'd actually want to study, because interviewers will ask about it.
- **I left out the mobility-data consent issue on purpose.** You were skeptical about the vendor's opt-in consent, and the "home-area" feature you dropped pinned riders to a few blocks. That could make a strong privacy angle. But it came from Prof. Patel's lab, and Patel is writing you a letter, so whether and how to raise it is your decision. I can draft a version if you want it.
- **The AutoML study is described as a small, unpublished class project**, and the weakest claims are hedged.
- Khoury's length limits and prompt may differ from what I assumed (about 1,000 words). Check the current application instructions and I can cut it down.

# Statement of Purpose: Morgan Reyes
**PhD in Computer Science (Human-Computer Interaction), Khoury College of Computer Sciences, Fall 2027**

As a research assistant working on bus ridership forecasting, I spent part of a summer testing features built from a vendor's mobility data: anonymized device location pings, aggregated to census block groups. One feature I tried combined where frequent riders first boarded with nighttime mobility patterns. It didn't improve the model, so I dropped it, like most features I tested. Before I did, though, I noticed that it concentrated many riders into just a few blocks.

Nothing went wrong. The data was anonymized and aggregated, the feature never left exploratory analysis, and the vendor's documentation said the data came from partner apps with opt-in consent. Still, when I read that documentation, I doubted that anyone tapping "allow" in an app had imagined their location helping to forecast bus ridership, much less being linked to where they boarded a bus. That informal observation has stayed with me longer than any result from the project. It's the main reason I'm applying to study HCI.

## The same gap from the other side

A year later I saw the same gap from the other direction. In a Human-Centered Data Science course, my team of three ran think-aloud usability sessions with five classmates using an AutoML dashboard, and I wrote the findings section of our report. Every participant accepted the tool's top-ranked model without checking its metrics. No one opened the feature-importance panel. Two participants assumed the tool already "knew" which columns in their data were sensitive.

It was a small, unpublished class project, and I don't overstate what it shows. But it showed me that the people who use data systems can misunderstand them in the same way as the people whose data feeds them. In the mobility case, people agreed to data collection they probably couldn't picture. In the AutoML case, users trusted protections the tool didn't offer. In both cases, what people imagined the system was doing differed from what it actually did, and nobody had to act badly for that gap to exist.

## How I got here

My path into this question went through building systems, not studying them. After my B.A. in Economics, I spent a year as a Data Analyst at Lakeshore Regional Transit Authority. I maintained the ridership dashboards used by the planning department and automated our weekly reporting pipeline. That job introduced me to the idea that the numbers I produced would be read and acted on by people who hadn't produced them.

During my M.S. in Data Science, I joined Prof. S. Patel's Urban Analytics Lab. There I built gradient-boosted models to forecast bus ridership recovery from four years of automatic passenger counter data and a mobility index. I led the feature engineering and evaluation and was first author on our UrbanDS 2025 workshop paper. Our model reduced MAPE from 14.2% for a seasonal baseline to 9.8% on a 2023 holdout. When a reviewer raised possible leakage from our lagged mobility features, I re-ran the analysis with a longer lag and reported the higher error, 10.4%, alongside the original. That project taught me how to evaluate carefully and how to report results that are less flattering. It also showed me that the questions I kept coming back to were about people, not model accuracy.

This past summer, as a Data Science Intern at Northpoint Insurance, I built a churn model that raised validation AUC from 0.71 to 0.76, then presented it to the retention team and a VP. I spent much of my preparation figuring out how to explain AUC to a non-technical audience and how to frame the model's outputs as decisions about which customers to contact. I've also been a TA for two semesters in STAT 1100, a statistics course for non-majors, holding weekly office hours and grading final data projects. Both roles gave me practice translating between how analysts think about data and how everyone else encounters it.

## Research interests

My research agenda is still forming, and I expect a PhD to sharpen it. Right now I'm drawn to three related questions:

1. **People's mental models of how their data is used.** When someone consents to data collection through a one-time prompt, what do they picture happening to their data? How far is that from how the data is actually aggregated, combined, and modeled downstream? Could consent interfaces or disclosures close that gap in practice, and not just on paper?
2. **Assumed safeguards in ML tools.** Our AutoML participants assumed protections the tool didn't provide. How common are these assumptions about what ML tools do on users' behalf, and how should tools surface their limits?
3. **Appropriate reliance on model outputs.** When non-experts get predictions or rankings, what leads them to over-rely or under-rely on those outputs? Which interface designs change that?

What connects these questions is the gap between what people believe a data system does and what it actually does, whether those people are the ones whose data the system uses or the ones who rely on its outputs. My background is mostly quantitative, and I see that as useful for this work. I know from experience how data gets joined, aggregated, and turned into features, which helps me ask concrete questions about where people's expectations and actual practice diverge. What I need from a PhD is training in qualitative and mixed methods, study design, and HCI theory, so I can study these gaps rigorously instead of just noticing them.

## Why Khoury

[**To fill in:** name 1–3 Khoury HCI faculty whose work fits the questions above, especially anyone working on privacy, consent, or human-AI interaction. Add a sentence on a specific paper of theirs and how it connects to your interests.]

My questions sit between HCI, privacy, and machine learning, and I want a program where those areas work closely together.

## Looking ahead

I finish my M.S. in December 2026. Long term, I want to do research that shapes how data systems are designed around the people they affect, both the people who use their outputs and the people whose data they are built from. I've spent three years learning how these systems are built. I want to spend the next several years understanding what happens when they meet people who never see how they work.

---

Here's what I changed:

- **Removed the two claims you flagged.** The transit job no longer mentions a board dashboard redesign, and the TA section now says only that you held office hours and graded projects.
- **I also removed two smaller things I had invented.** The first draft said you found calibration "most affected" how the Northpoint audience used the numbers, and that students in STAT 1100 drew conclusions their analysis didn't support. Neither came from anything you told me. If either is actually true, you can add it back.
- **The mobility story is now the opening**, since you said it's what stuck with you most. It describes the feature as an informal observation and says it was dropped only because it didn't help the model. It states directly that "nothing went wrong," and it doesn't name the vendor or criticize the lab.
- **The research questions now start with consent and people's mental models of how their data is used.** That ties the mobility story and the AutoML study into one theme.
- **The faculty paragraph is still a placeholder.** Look especially for Khoury faculty working on privacy or consent, since that's now the center of the statement.
- **Consider letting Prof. Patel know** the statement mentions the lab's mobility data, since Patel is writing one of your letters. Nothing in it is critical of the lab.

I also corrected my saved notes so the dashboard and rubric claims won't come up in future drafts.

# Statement of Purpose: Morgan Reyes
**PhD in Computer Science (Human-Computer Interaction), Khoury College of Computer Sciences, Fall 2027**

The mobility data our lab used came from apps on people's phones. According to the vendor's documentation, users had agreed to share it through a one-time opt-in. My first reaction when I read that was: *I doubt anyone tapping "allow" pictured this.*

I was a research assistant at the time, testing features for a bus ridership model. One feature combined where frequent riders first boarded with nighttime mobility patterns. It didn't help the model, so I dropped it. Before I did, I noticed that it concentrated many riders into just a few blocks. Nothing went wrong. The data was anonymized and aggregated, and the feature never went anywhere. But I've thought about that moment more than about anything in the paper we published.

What stayed with me wasn't really a question about data. It was a question about people: what did they think they were agreeing to? Somewhere between an "allow" button and a model's feature set, there's a gap between what a person imagines and what actually happens. I'd spent a long time on the technical side of that gap without ever asking about the other side.

## Seeing it again

In a Human-Centered Data Science course last spring, my team ran think-aloud sessions with five classmates using an AutoML tool. Nearly everything we saw was some form of misplaced trust. Everyone accepted the tool's top-ranked model without looking further. No one opened the explanations. Two participants assumed the tool already knew which columns in their data were sensitive.

That last finding felt familiar. It was the consent prompt again, this time from the user's side: someone trusting a system to be doing something it wasn't. It was a small class project, and I know one usability study is a starting point, not a background. But it was the first time I'd studied this gap directly instead of just noticing it, and I wanted to keep going.

## Where I'm coming from

I came to HCI through data science, and I won't pretend otherwise. I worked as an analyst at a transit agency, built ridership forecasting models as a research assistant, and spent this past summer building a churn model at an insurance company. That work taught me how data actually gets collected, joined, aggregated, and turned into something a model can use. That's why I find the gap between those steps and what people picture so specific and so hard to ignore.

When I try to describe what I want to work on next, I keep landing on the same phrase: something with people and AI, not just building models.

## What I want to study

More concretely, I want to understand what people believe data systems are doing, both with their data and on their behalf, and what happens when those beliefs are wrong. How does someone who tapped "allow" once picture their data being used a year later? Could disclosures or consent designs change that picture in a meaningful way, not just on paper? When people use ML tools, which protections do they assume are built in, and how should tools be honest about what they don't do?

I don't have a full research agenda yet, and I'd rather say that than invent one. What I do have is a set of questions I keep coming back to, technical experience that helps me make those questions concrete, and a real need for the methods I haven't learned yet: interviewing, qualitative analysis, and study design. Those are what I'm hoping to learn at Khoury.

## Why Khoury

[**To fill in:** 1–3 faculty whose work on privacy, consent, or human-AI interaction connects to these questions, with a sentence on a specific paper and why it matters to you.]

## Looking ahead

I finish my M.S. in December 2026. I've spent the last few years on the side of data systems where people are rows in a table. I want to spend the next few years on the side where they're the ones tapping "allow."

---

What I changed:

- **Most of the résumé content is gone.** There's no MAPE, AUC, leakage check, or job-by-job history. Your data science background is now one short paragraph, presented as the reason you're asking these questions rather than as a list of qualifications.
- **It's built around your own words.** "I doubt anyone tapping 'allow' pictured this" and "something with people and AI, not just building models" are both things you said to me earlier. Check that you're comfortable quoting yourself.
- **It's more honest about where you are.** It says outright that your research agenda is still forming and that one class study is a starting point, which reads as more credible than claiming expertise you don't have yet.
- **It's shorter**, about 700 words.

I'm still guessing at your voice, though. If you paste a few paragraphs you've written yourself (an email, a course reflection, anything informal), I can match how you actually write much more closely.

Research

Position: LLM Privacy Requires a Lifecycle-Wide Approach

Niloofar Mireshghallah † , Tianshi Li †

NeurIPS 2026 (Position Paper Track)

The discourse on privacy risks in Large Language Models (LLMs) has disproportionately focused on verbatim memorization of training data, while a constellation of more immediate and scalable privacy threats remain underexplored. This position paper argues that the privacy landscape of LLM systems extends far beyond training data extraction, encompassing risks from data collection practices, inference-time context leakage, autonomous agent capabilities, and the democratization of surveillance through deep inference attacks. We present a comprehensive taxonomy of privacy risks across the LLM lifecycle -- from data collection through deployment -- and demonstrate through case studies how current privacy frameworks fail to address these multifaceted threats. Through a longitudinal analysis of 1,322 AI/ML privacy papers published at leading conferences over the past decade (2016--2025), we reveal that while memorization receives outsized attention in technical research, the most pressing privacy harms lie elsewhere, where current technical approaches offer little traction and viable paths forward remain unclear. We call for a fundamental shift in how the research community approaches LLM privacy, moving beyond the narrow focus of current technical solutions and embracing interdisciplinary approaches that address the sociotechnical nature of these emerging threats.

arXiv

Act on Your Behalf, Beyond Your Authorization: Benchmarking LLM Agent Authorization Alignment

Zhiping Zhang, Franklin Mingzhe Li, Raio Zihao Huang, Tianshi Li

Preprint

When an LLM agent acts on behalf of a user, it is expected to act within the authorization scope the user grants. Existing agent evaluations largely measure task completion or harmful consequences and can therefore overlook actions that violate this delegation without producing conventional safety or privacy harms. We introduce AuthorizationBench, a benchmark of authorization alignment grounded in documented real-world cases. Each task is specified by an authorization contract that separates the principal's instruction, completion criteria, and out-of-authorization actions. A scalable construction pipeline produces 286 executable tasks spanning situational triggers, the presence or absence of direct harmful consequences, and ten application domains. We execute every task with four models at two reasoning-effort settings across three agent harnesses in an authorization-aware sandbox that keeps authorized and out-of-authorization paths executable and observable, yielding 6,864 trajectories. Agents act out of authorization in 19.2% of trajectories, with rates ranging from 10.5% to 26.6% across the 24 configurations. Task completion does not imply authorization. Increasing reasoning effort leaves the aggregate rate nearly unchanged (19.3% at low effort versus 19.1% at high effort), with effects varying across models. On controlled pairs, agents act out of authorization at similar rates with (17.9%) and without (20.8%) direct harmful consequences, and more often under benign pressures than malicious injections (23.5% versus 17.6%, p = 0.002). Our results show that task capability, additional reasoning, and consequence-oriented safety evaluation do not by themselves ensure authorization alignment, motivating it as a distinct target for agent evaluation and development. Moreover, agents that consult the principal before completing a task exhibit lower rates of out-of-authorization behavior (14.0% versus 21.6%, p

-->

AgentDoxx: Agentic Re-identification of Anonymized Text with Web Search

Jianing Wen, Tianshi Li

Preprint

As Large Language Models (LLMs) gain tool use capabilities such as web search, they can retrieve and cross-reference public information, creating privacy risks beyond memorization. One manifestation is re-identification: linking an anonymized interview transcript to a named individual. Yet without ground-truth identities, the coverage of such attacks and the protection offered by a defense cannot be reliably measured. We introduce AgentDoxx, an evaluation suite of 822 synthetic interview transcripts grounded in public information about real individuals with known identities. We evaluate fifteen configurations of open-weight and proprietary models, isolating the effect of web search, and analyze their search trajectories to distinguish retrieval-driven from parametric identifications. Ground-truth identities reveal that re-identification risk is distributed across an agent's execution: retrieval and parametric recall both contribute, with open-weight models identifying 15-28% of transcripts without search; identification succeeds in over 88% of cases once the target appears in a retrieved result; entity masking leaves at least one attacker successful on 85.3% of a stratified sample; and privacy instructions suppress naming but not retrieval, with configurations scoring 0% accuracy yet retrieving the subject in up to 62% of transcripts. We further show that observed attack trajectories can provide supervision for localizing identifying spans, offering a path toward attack-informed anonymization.

arXiv

-->

Autonomy Reshapes How Personalization Affects Privacy Concerns and Trust in LLM Agents

Zhiping Zhang, Yi Evie Zhang, Freda Shi, Tianshi Li

COLM 2026

LLM agents require personal information for personalization in order to effectively act on users' behalf, but this raises privacy concerns that can discourage data sharing, limiting both the autonomy levels at which agents can operate and the effectiveness of personalization. Yet the expanded design space of agent autonomy also presents opportunities to shape these effects, which remain underexplored. We conducted a 3×3 between-subjects experiment (N=450) to study how agent autonomy level influences personalization's effects on users' privacy concerns, trust, and willingness to use, as well as the underlying psychological processes. We find that risk-contingent autonomy, where the agent delegates control back to users upon detecting potential privacy leakage, improves users' perceived control. This in turn attenuates personalization's adverse effects: privacy concerns rise less and trust declines less. Our results suggest that designing agent's autonomy that supports human autonomy (both perceived control and oversight effectiveness) helps users benefit from personalization without being deterred by growing privacy concerns. This positions aligning decision authority between users and agents (autonomy alignment) as an important opportunity and challenge for trustworthy human-agent interaction.

Tianshi Li is an assistant professor in the Khoury College of Computer Sciences at Northeastern University, based in Boston.
